newsitem.title: POLAND: Liberal Polish farm minister Jagielinski sacked.
newsitem.headline: Liberal Polish farm minister Jagielinski sacked.

text.p: Poland's Peasant Party, rebelling against a government drive to consolidate small farms into larger, more efficient units, forced Agriculture Minister Roman Jagielinski out of office on Thursday.

Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz had struggled for weeks to keep Jagielinski, a member of the Peasant Party's liberal wing whose modernising, market-oriented policies were praised by Western diplomats keen to see Poland preparing itself for future membership of the European Union.

But the coalition agreement which holds Poland's government together gives the Peasants the right to name the farm minister and Cimoszewicz, bowing to the demands of a majority in the party leadership, finally asked President Aleksander Kwasniewski to dismiss Jagielinski as farm minister and deputy prime minister.
No replacement was named and a government source said the post was likely to remain vacant for some time.

The Peasants' leadership wants Jaroslaw Kalinowski, a little-known, 35-year-old politician, to get the job but Cimoszewicz, who belongs to the larger party in the ruling coalition, has opposed the choice.
"Until the coalition parties sort things out...one of the current deputy ministers will be the acting minister," said the source, who asked not to be named.
"It is my deepest conviction that Roman Jagielinski has been the best agriculture minister for many years. His departure is a great loss," Cimoszewicz told parliament.
"I submitted a motion (to dismiss Jagielinski) only because under the coalition agreement his party has the right to designate the minister," he added.
Peasant leaders grouped round party chief Waldemar Pawlak, favour the interests of small farm owners who are keen to uphold state protection of agriculture.
They have in recent months attacked Jagielinski who ran unsuccessfully for the party leadership last year.
They accused him of policies resulting in a food trade deficit last year and low grain prices for domestic farmers, allegations which many economic analysts said were unfounded.

European Union diplomats have praised Jagielinski for his plans to modernise the countryside, encourage larger, more efficient holdings and cut the number of farms from more than two million to below one million.
Poland's obsolete agriculture is seen as a major hurdle to the country's accession to the EU.
Jagielinki suggested on Thursday some members of his own party were hampering the much-needed agricultural reform because it was unpopular among the party's backers who were small farmers.

"If I faced opposition in this parliament, this was predominantly opposition from within my own party... I have subscribed to the view that where the state's interest is at stake the party's interest ends and now I am suffering consequences," he told parliament.
Cimoszewicz -- of the coalition's more pro-market party, the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance -- has tried to defend Jagielinski and delayed his dismissal for weeks.
He finally bowed to pressure when the Peasants began to block the coalition's work by failing to attend meetings.
But Cimoszewicz's refusal to name Kalinowski the new farm minister might stir another conflict in the coalition, which has lasted nearly four years despite frequent disputes.

Analysts say the coalition should hold until parliamentary elections due around September, in which rightist and centrist parties rooted in the Solidarity movement will challenge the ex-communists and Peasants.
